itens.t: Software failure interrupts BepiColombo spacecraft's arrival at Mercury
itens.r: A software malfunction has complicated the long-awaited arrival of the two-billion-dollar BepiColombo spacecraft at Mercury, leaving engineers scrambling for solutions. The ambitious mission, a joint project between European and Japanese space agencies, faced unexpected hurdles just as it reached the inner planet. Ground teams are currently analyzing telemetry data to assess the probe's systems following the critical interruption. Further updates on the spacecraft's operational status are expected as engineers work to stabilize the trajectory.
itens.d:
The BepiColombo spacecraft's long-awaited arrival at Mercury faced serious trouble last week after a software failure interrupted its critical orbital insertion. Following an eight-year journey, the joint European and Japanese probe entered a scheduled communication blackout while positioning its thrusters 635 kilometers above the planet's surface.

Tension mounted at the European Space Agency operations center in Germany when the planned 37-minute thruster burn ended prematurely after only 28 minutes. Mission control realized something was wrong when a signal was received much earlier than anticipated, leaving engineers searching for answers regarding the spacecraft's stability.
itens.e:
The BepiColombo spacecraft encountered serious trouble last week during its long-awaited arrival at Mercury following a software failure that interrupted its critical orbital insertion. After an eight-year journey, the joint European and Japanese probe entered a scheduled communication blackout while positioning its thrusters 635 kilometers above the planet's surface. Tension mounted at the European Space Agency operations center in Germany when the planned 37-minute thruster burn ended prematurely after only 28 minutes, prompting mission control to realize something was wrong when a signal arrived much earlier than anticipated.

This incident directly impacts the engineers and scientific teams at the European Space Agency who are now left searching for answers regarding the spacecraft's stability after the unexpected interruption. One risk is that such technical failures could compromise the mission's primary objectives after years of interplanetary travel, threatening the collection of vital data from Mercury. This suggests that deep-space orbital maneuvers remain fraught with unpredictable hazards even at the final stages of a scheduled planetary arrival.

What to watch next is how mission control addresses the software failure and whether engineers can successfully verify the spacecraft's stability following the premature thruster burn. Observers will also be monitoring future updates from the European Space Agency regarding adjustments to the probe's trajectory and overall health. Further announcements will likely clarify the extent of the delay and the viability of the remaining mission timeline.

itens.t: Astronomers witness red giant star consume smaller companion star
itens.r: Astronomers have captured the rare event of a red giant star devouring its smaller stellar companion in a cosmic feeding frenzy. Researchers expressed astonishment at observing the stellar cannibalism in real time.
itens.d:
Astronomers have witnessed a rare cosmic event where a red giant star consumed its smaller companion star. The cannibalistic star, nicknamed "Big Bao," is roughly 350 times larger than the sun and devoured its companion, affectionately called "Little Bao."

The merger event, officially designated AT2025abao, was tracked using an array of ground- and space-based telescopes, including the James Webb Space Telescope. The spectacular cosmic indigestion concluded with a massive eruption captured by Palomar Observatory instruments.
